title: MA7-05107
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The claimants, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, a citizen of Peru, and her son, XXXXX XXXXX, an American citizen, are claiming refugee protection in Canada, under section 96 and paragraphs 97(1)(a) and 97(1)(b)1 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
The principal claimant was named designated representative for her minor son, the claimant.
Here is a summary of the claimants' allegations as they appear in their Personal Information Form (PIF).

The principal claimant entered into a conjugal relationship with a Peruvian XXXXX XXXXX when she was 16 years old. They lived together for four months in 2001. Shortly after they started living together, it became apparent that her partner was a violent person with many faults, including a gambling addiction, alcoholism, committing illicit activities and drug use. He mistreated the female claimant on many occasions. She then left him and soon after met the father of her son, the claimant. They both left Peru in 2002, when the female claimant was already pregnant with the latter. They split up after arriving in the United States. In early 2007, the female claimant met a new partner. This one threatened to kill her and so the female claimant filed a complaint with the police. He was arrested by the authorities and incarcerated. The female claimant, who learned from other people that he was threatening her from his jail cell, decided that she and her son should come join members of her family in Canada in July 2007.
The claimants' identities have been established to the panel's satisfaction by the documents submitted on file.2

Having analyzed the documentary and testimonial evidence, and having taken into consideration Guideline 4: Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution, the panel determines that the claimants are not "Convention refugees" or "persons in need of protection" for the following reasons.
The male claimant, who is an American citizen, did not present any evidence related to the United States.
The principal claimant was not credible.
There were many contradictions in her testimony.

The panel asked the female claimant whether she knew of any other sources of income for her former partner, other than that earned as a XXXXX XXXXX. She stated that [translation] "no, he did not have any other sources of income". When asked why, in that case, she had indicated in her PIF that she has discovered that most of his income came from sources other than his XXXXX work, she replied that she was confused and that, at the end of their cohabitation, she found out that he was involved in something questionable, but that she was not certain whether it was drugs. The panel rejects this explanation that is not an explanation. If, according to her PIF, the female claimant was aware that her former partner's income came from sources other than his legitimate work, she would not have answered that way, that he had no other sources of income, and then state that he was involved in something questionable, but that she was not certain whether it was drugs. This is not credible.

The female claimant stated that her former partner was drunk when he came home. When asked whether he was under the influence of any other substance when he came home, she stated that she could not tell because she is not familiar with drugs. The panel then pointed out to the female claimant that it is written in her PIF that whenever he arrived home under the influence of drugs, she had to endure his abuse. She replied that she does not recognize the characteristics of drugs and that he might have been under the influence of drugs. She added that his friends allegedly told her that he took drugs. The panel rejects the female claimant's explanations, which do not explain in any way why, if she is not familiar with the characteristics of drugs and is therefore unable to determine whether her partner was under the influence of drugs, she would have stated in her PIF that he abused her when he arrived home under the influence of drugs. Furthermore, in her testimony, she was not able to state spontaneously that he took drugs. The panel is of the opinion that this was added to the female claimant's PIF in order to improve her story. This is not credible.

The female claimant stated that her former partner was often drunk. When asked what other faults this former partner had, other than taking drugs and drinking alcohol, she stated that that was all. The panel pointed out to the female claimant that she indicated in her PIF that this former partner also gambled. The female claimant stated that she forgot to mention it. Once again, the panel is of the opinion that this factor was added to the female claimant's narrative in order to improve it. This is not credible.

The female claimant also stated that her grandmother told her in XXXXX 2002, while she was in the United States, that her former partner was looking for her. Once again, in 2005, her grandmother allegedly told her that he wanted to know where the female claimant was. When asked why this information was not in her PIF, she replied that she did not know why she did not include it. The panel is of the opinion that this answer is not satisfactory. This is important information that should have been included in the female claimant's PIF, as it corroborates the persecuting agent's bad intentions, in spite of the nine years that have passed since they separated. If the female claimant had in fact received this information from her grandmother, the panel is of the opinion that she would not have forgotten to write it in her PIF. This all undermines the female claimant's testimony.

The female claimant also stated that she only went to the police once to file a complaint. However, it is written in her PIF that the female claimant went to see the police for the first time and was told that she needed proof. She then allegedly went to another police station to ask for protection, but she was refused. When asked about the disparity between her testimony, where she stated that she only went to the police once, and her PIF, where it is written that she went twice, she stated that she did not remember because she wrote it in her PIF a long time ago. The panel is of the opinion that this explanation is not credible. If the female claimant had in fact been to the police twice and she had pointed it out when writing her PIF in 2007, she would have been able to repeat it at her hearing, instead of replying that it had been a long time since she had read her PIF. The panel is of the opinion, once again, that these facts were added to the female claimant's PIF in order to improve her story. All of this is not credible.

At the port of entry, in the document Schedule 1 Background Information, which she completed on the day of her arrival,3 the female claimant provided the name of the person that she met in the United States whom she had had incarcerated because he was abusing her. In that document, she did not indicate that she also feared her former Peruvian partner. When asked about this omission, the female claimant replied that she confused the name of her former partner in Peru and that of the one living in the United States. The panel is of the opinion that this explanation is not credible. The female claimant had specifically mentioned in that document, and on the same page, that she feared returning to Peru, not the United States. The female claimant therefore understood that she had to identify the person that she feared in Peru, which she was not able to do. This is not credible.

The dates and addresses that the female claimant provided in her PIF and Schedule 1 Background Information as periods of cohabitation do not correspond with the female claimant's testimony. In question 3 of her PIF, she indicated that she and her former spouse became common-law partners on XXXXX, 2001. In her testimony, she stated that she met him in XXXXX or XXXXX 2001 and that she went to live with him in XXXXX 2001. When asked what she had indicated in her PIF as the beginning of their cohabitation, she replied that it was not exact, but she had provided no explanation as to why she had put XXXXX, 2001, in her PIF. This is not credible.

When asked why, at her port of entry interview,4 it is indicated that she allegedly lived with this former partner for one year-and not five or six months, as she testified-she stated that she had no comments. All of this is not credible.

When the female claimant was asked why she had not ever indicated, in her PIF or in her immigration documents, that she had lived with this former partner at XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, she stated that she did not think that it was necessary since she lived there for a brief period of time. The panel is of the opinion that this explanation is not credible. In fact, the female claimant claimed refugee protection in Canada because she was afraid of her former common-law partner, with whom she had lived. Had this actually been the case, the panel is of the opinion that the female claimant would have made a point of specifying, in the immigration documents as well as in her PIF for the questions regarding addresses, that she had lived at XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, instead of indicating her grandmother's address. All of this undermines the female claimant's credibility.
Consequently, the panel does not believe the principal claimant's story and problems, and is of the opinion that she invented a story in order to obtain refugee status in Canada.

The principal claimant might well have had problems of domestic violence in the United States with a Guatemalan partner, as per her testimony, but the panel is of the opinion that this factor has no nexus with the female claimant's fear of being persecuted in Peru. No evidence was presented to support the contention that her problems of domestic violence in the United States with another partner, other than her form Peruvian partner, could lead to a fear of persecution in Peru.

No evidence was presented related to a fear of returning to the United States in regards to XXXXX XXXXX, who is an American citizen. Consequently, the panel determines that his claim cannot be considered under section 96, or paragraphs 97(1)(a) and 97(1)(b) of the IRPA.

For these reasons, the panel determines that the claimants, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, a citizen of Peru, and her son, XXXXX XXXXX, an American citizen, are not "Convention refugees" or "persons in need of protection".

Consequently, their claim for refugee protection in Canada is rejected. Roxane Cyr Roxane Cyr March 9, 2010 Date IRB translation Original language: French REFUGEE PROTECTION DIVISION / DOMESTIC VIOLENCE / NEXUS / SOJOURNING / CONTRADICTIONS / CREDIBLE BASIS / FEMALE / NEGATIVE / PERU 1 97. (1) A person in need of protection is a person in Canada whose removal to their country or countries of nationality or, if they do not have a country of nationality, their country of former habitual residence, would subject them personally (a) to a danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture within the meaning of Article 1 of the Convention Against Torture; or (b) to a risk to their life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment if (i) the person is unable or, because of that risk, unwilling to avail themself of the protection of that country, (ii) the risk would be faced by the person in every part of that country and is not faced generally by other individuals in or from that country, (iii) the risk is not inherent or incidental to lawful sanctions, unless imposed in disregard of accepted international standards, and (iv) the risk is not caused by the inability of that country to provide adequate health or medical care. 2 Exhibit A-2: Immigration documents. 3 Idem. 4 Idem. --------------- --------------- --------------- --------------- RPD File No. / No de dossier de la SPR : MA7-05107 MA7-04202 7
